entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 21 Is 21:1-10 . Repetition of the Assurance Given in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Chapters to the Jews About to Be Captives in Babylon, that Their Enemy Should Be Destroyed and They Be Delivered. He does not narrate the event, but graphically supposes himself a watchman in Babylon, beholding the events as they pass. 1. desert-- the champaign between Babylon and Persia; it was once a desert, and it was to become so again. of the sea-- The plain was covered with the water of the Euphrates like a "sea" ( Jr 51:13 , 36 ; so Is 11:15 , the Nile), until Semiramis raised great dams against it. Cyrus removed these dykes, and so converted the whole country again into a vast desert marsh. whirlwinds in the south-- ( Job 37:9 ; Zec 9:14 ). The south wind comes upon Babylon from the deserts of Arabia, and its violence is the greater from its course being unbroken along the plain ( Job 1:19 ). desert-- the plain between Babylon and Persia. terrible land-- Media; to guard against which was the object of Nitocris' great works [Herodotus, 1.185]. Compare as to "terrible" applied to a wilderness, as being full of unknown dangers, De 1:29 .

It may be translated, "is repaid with treachery"; then the subject of the verb is Babylon. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8679"/><div sID="gen14325" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8679"/><hi type="bold">4. panted--</hi>"is bewildered" [Barnes].<div eID="gen14325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14326" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night of my pleasure--</hi>The prophet supposes himself one of the banqueters at Belshazzar's feast, on the night that Babylon was about to be taken by surprise; hence his expression, "my pleasure" (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Is 14:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.39">Jr 51:39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.1-Dan.5.31">Da 5:1-31</reference>). <div eID="gen14326" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8680"/><div sID="gen14327" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8680"/><hi type="bold">5. Prepare the table--</hi>namely, the feast in Babylon; during which Cyrus opened the dykes made by Semiramis to confine the Euphrates to one channel and suffered them to overflow the country, so that he could enter Babylon by the channel of the river. Isaiah first represents the king ordering the feast to be got ready. The suddenness of the irruption of the foe is graphically expressed by the rapid turn in the language to an alarm addressed to the Babylonian princes, "Arise," &c. (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.22.13">Is 22:13</reference>). Maurer translates, "They prepare the table," &c. But see <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Is 8:9</reference>.<div eID="gen14327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">watch in ... watchtower--</hi>rather, "set the watch." This done, they thought they might feast in entire security. Babylon had many watchtowers on its walls.<div eID="gen14328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">anoint ... shield--</hi>This was done to prevent the leather of the shield becoming hard and liable to crack. "Make ready for defense"; the mention of the "shield" alone implies that it is the Babylonian revellers who are called on to prepare for instant self-defense. Horsley translates, "Grip the oiled shield." <div eID="gen14329" type="x-p"/>

Go, set a watchman, let him declare what he seeth--</hi>God's direction to Isaiah to set a watchman to "declare" what he sees. But as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Is 21:10</reference>, Isaiah himself is represented as the one who "declared." Horsley makes him the "watchman," and translates, "Come, let him who standeth on the watchtower report what he seeth." <div eID="gen14330" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8682"/><div sID="gen14331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8682"/><hi type="bold">7. chariot, &c.--</hi>rather, "a body of riders," namely, some riding in pairs on horses (literally, "pairs of horsemen," that is, two abreast), others on asses, others on camels (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>). "Chariot" is not appropriate to be joined, as English Version translates, with "asses"; the Hebrew means plainly in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>, "a body of men riding." The Persians used asses and camels for war [Maurer]. Horsley translates, "One drawn in a car, with a pair of riders, drawn by an ass, drawn by a camel"; Cyrus is the man; the car drawn by a camel and ass yoked together and driven by two postilions, one on each, is the joint army of Medes and Persians under their respective leaders. He thinks the more ancient military cars were driven by men riding on the beasts that drew them; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference> favors this. <div eID="gen14331" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8683"/><div sID="gen14332" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8683"/><hi type="bold">8. A lion--</hi>rather, "(The watchman) cried, I am as a lion"; so as is understood (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Is 62:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference>). The point of comparison to "a lion" is in <reference osisRef="Rev.10.3">Re 10:3</reference>, the loudness of the cry. But here it is rather his vigilance. The lion's eyelids are short, so that, even when asleep, he seems to be on the watch, awake; hence he was painted on doors of temples as the symbol of watchfulness, guarding the place (Hor. Apollo) [Horsley]. <div eID="gen14332" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8684"/><div sID="gen14333" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8684"/><hi type="bold">9. chariot of men--</hi>chariots with men in them; or rather, the same body of riders, horsemen two abreast, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference> [Maurer]. But Horsley, "The man drawn in a car with a pair of riders." The first half of this verse describes what the watchman sees; the second half, what the watchman says, in consequence of what he sees. In the interval between <reference osisRef="Isa.21.7">Is 21:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Is 21:9</reference>, the overthrow of Babylon by the horsemen, or man in the car, is accomplished. The overthrow needed to be announced to the prophet by the watchman, owing to the great extent of the city. Herodotus (1.131) says that one part of the city was captured some time before the other received the tidings of it.<div eID="gen14333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answered--</hi>not to something said previously, but in reference to the subject in the mind of the writer, to be collected from the preceding discourse: proclaimeth (<reference osisRef="Job.3.2">Job 3:2</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Dan.2.26">Da 2:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.8">Ac 5:8</reference>).<div eID="gen14334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fallen ... fallen--</hi>The repetition expresses emphasis and certainty (<reference osisRef="Ps.92.9">Psa 92:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.93.3">93:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.8">Jr 51:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.18.2">Re 18:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14336" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">images--</hi>Bel, Merodach, &c. (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.2">Jr 50:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.44">51:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.52">52</reference>). The Persians had no images, temples, or altars, and charged the makers of such with madness [Herodotus 1.131]; therefore they dashed the Babylonian "images broken unto the ground." <div eID="gen14336" type="x-p"/>

navigation_sections.content_plain: CHAPTER 21 Is 21:1-10 . Repetition of the Assurance Given in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Chapters to the Jews About to Be Captives in Babylon, that Their Enemy Should Be Destroyed and They Be Delivered.
